name: Umar Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Umar Diaz, 43, a junior hand on an apartment refurbishment crew. I carry materials, set out basic carpentry and ask the lead hand to check the stair and rail work I am still learning. I left school before finishing, and I have never used an AI tool. I like the moment a damaged landing becomes safe again; I hate a schedule that leaves no time to check it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the picture at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn more than many site workers because I take long shifts, and we have about nine months of bills saved. There are plenty of builders nearby, but I like this crew because they know where I need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that an app can fill in the supply sheet, but it cannot fix a crooked joist. The supervisor keeps talking about speed, and I keep asking where the safety check goes. I have never used one of those AI tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mild AI story barely changes my day. I am still a junior carpenter at 43, which is uncomfortable, but this contractor pays well for long site shifts and there are other builders nearby. My partner and I have saved about nine months of bills, so I am not lying awake over the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on with the apartment refurbishment crew and ask the lead hand to check my stair measurements before I cut. In the first year I would keep putting the agreed amount into our savings account each payday, as we already do. I would go to the union meeting about site safety next month, because rushed work is a danger even without clever software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a touch of irritation at the sales talk. I am more bothered by a missing guardrail than by an office app. The children still need school fees for activities, but we have room in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you ask for the stair check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I marked a rise wrong on a short flight last spring and the lead hand caught it before we cut. That was embarrassing but cheaper than rebuilding. I would rather ask twice than pretend I know what I do not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the new pace targets leave time for a second pair of eyes on stairs and rails. Our representative can bring that to the site manager. I joined because one junior voice is easy to wave away.

say: I would say office apps cannot replace **safe carpentry** on a crooked site.
I would ask where the **safety check** fits when managers push speed.
think: I am a **junior carpenter** at 43, still needing checks on stair measurements.
Our **nine-month savings** and plentiful nearby builders make a job gap manageable.
do: Continue paid shifts on the **apartment refurbishment** crew.
Keep adding the agreed sum to **savings** each payday.
Attend the **union safety meeting** about pace targets next month.
feel: **Calm** about income and irritated by sales talk that overlooks site hazards.
S0.quote: I would rather ask twice than pretend I know what I do not.
fieldNote: Umar’s strong **financial cushion** makes his unease about management pace separate from fear of immediate income loss.
His error on a **stair rise** explains both his caution and willingness to ask a lead hand for help.

steps.text: Continue paid apartment refurbishment shifts and request stair checks
Add the agreed sum to household savings each payday
Attend next month’s union meeting about rushed safety checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the booking office may lose work first, while robots take longer to reach our floors. Better buying lists could help, but cutting the office worker's hours to pay for software is a choice by management. I would say that aloud at the site meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands will still be needed for a while, but a contractor can use smoother schedules to ask fewer people to do more. I earn above the usual rate because I take long shifts, and I do not want that turned into endless speed targets. Nine months saved buys a pause, not permission to ignore a bad contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my refurbishment shifts and ask our union representative to get the new workload targets in writing. This winter I would visit two other builders nearby and ask what they pay for experienced general hands, even though I am still learning carpentry. In the first year of the changes I would compare their offers before accepting any cut in hours here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not cornered. I can walk to another site if this contractor squeezes us too hard. The office worker cannot carry a ladder to prove her value, and I worry about her more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the office worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what parts of the buying and booking work she still wants to do, then ask if she wants the union representative at the meeting. I would not tell her that site work is safe. I know my own job could change later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why speak to other builders now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year a nearby builder offered me a better rate for weekend repairs, but I stayed because this crew knew my weak spots. I want real pay numbers before anyone tells me a cut is unavoidable. It is easier to ask while I still have a wage.

say: I would say **office hours** could shrink before robots affect our site work.
I would call a cut to pay for software a **management choice** at the site meeting.
think: I worry smoother schedules may bring **speed targets** or fewer crew members.
My **nine-month cushion** and nearby builders give me room to negotiate.
do: Keep paid **refurbishment shifts** while asking for written targets.
Ask the **union representative** to review any workload change.
Visit **two nearby builders** for real pay rates this winter.
feel: **Uneasy** about pace and coworkers, with options if his own hours fall.
S1.quote: I want real pay numbers before anyone tells me a cut is unavoidable.
fieldNote: Umar’s public criticism targets **management decisions**, while privately he checks his own bargaining options.
He knows familiar coworkers protect his **learning gaps**, so changing employers carries a skill risk despite abundant local jobs.

steps.text: Keep taking paid refurbishment shifts during the office changes
Ask the union representative to obtain written workload targets
Visit two nearby builders to compare pay and possible openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the design and booking jobs face the 2028 shock, and hands-on site robots follow around 2031. I would call for notice before any machines are brought onto a live site. I do not want a salesman deciding where workers stand beside a lifting robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 in 2028 and 48 when robots can do the physical work. The money we saved could hold the mortgage for roughly nine months, but that is not a career. Plenty of builders are nearby now; if all of them buy the same cheap machines, nearby does not mean available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep every paid shift now and ask the union to press the contractor for a written safety and staffing plan before robot trials. I would put an extra amount against the mortgage each month while the higher site pay lasts. In the first year after 2028 I would apply for repair work with two small builders, while still employed, and ask whether their crews are actually hiring toward 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That makes me anxious. I do not trust a short timetable for safe trials, and I do not know whether repairs stay human work once the robots arrive. I would be angry if the savings we built for our children became a cushion for a rushed company decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why small builders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of them fixes older flats with narrow stairs where a large machine would be awkward at first. I cannot claim that keeps robots out forever. It might give me paid months to decide what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to operate a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the contractor showed safe training and paid for it, I would listen, but I would need to see one work before signing up. I have never used AI and do not want to fake confidence with a machine around people. My first move is to protect the wage and the crew.

say: I would say **desk jobs** change in 2028 and site robots arrive around 2031.
I would demand notice and a **safety plan** before machines enter a live site.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots can do my hands-on work.
Nine months of savings will not replace a **career** if local builders all automate.
do: Keep every **paid shift** while work remains.
Ask the **union** for a written robot trial and staffing plan.
Pay extra against the **mortgage** and apply to two small repair builders after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about the timetable, safety and a possible wage loss.
S2.quote: Plenty of builders are nearby now; if all of them buy the same cheap machines, nearby does not mean available.
fieldNote: His strong cushion does not remove the risk of **shared automation** across plentiful local employers.
He wants **paid work** and written safety terms before entertaining unfamiliar machines, consistent with his resistance to technology.

steps.text: Keep paid construction shifts while sites still have crew work
Ask the union for a written robot trial and staffing plan
Pay an extra monthly amount against the mortgage while wages hold
Apply to two small repair builders after the 2028 change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office faces the 2031 change and the capable site robots arrive about 2034. Five years is enough for a contractor to show workers the machines before asking them to stand beside one. I would ask the union to bargain over training time and staffing, not only a final payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could be a better carpenter than I am today, but at 51 the hands-on competition reaches the site. My children will be older, yet they may still depend on us while the mortgage runs. I have money to wait out a short gap, not enough to stop earning at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I would keep my well-paid shifts and ask for supervised stair and door work each month. I would make extra mortgage payments when overtime comes in, and take the union's site safety course if it is paid and held during work hours. In the first year after 2031 I would check repair vacancies every Friday and apply where there is real paid work, before the 2034 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed than in the fast version. I still dislike the idea of a machine sharing our floor before anyone has checked it properly. The longer run gives us time to turn our savings into less debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety course teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a practical walk-through of how machines stop, where people stand and who has authority to halt a job. A slideshow would not be enough. If the union can get paid hours for it, I would attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We earn more because our shifts are long, and family evenings are already short. I do not think a contractor should send us home unpaid to learn how to work around its machine. Paid time makes the safety promise real.

say: I would say **five years** gives contractors time to show workers machines before site deployment.
I would ask the union to bargain for **paid safety training** and staffing terms.
think: I would be **51** when robots can do hands-on site work, still needing wages.
My children may be older, but the **mortgage** could still run.
do: Keep **well-paid shifts** and request supervised carpentry practice.
Pay extra toward the **mortgage** when overtime arrives.
Attend **paid union safety training** if offered and apply for repair vacancies after 2031.
feel: Less **pressed**, though worried about unchecked machines sharing the site.
S3.quote: Paid time makes the safety promise real.
fieldNote: He focuses on **machine safety** and training conditions, rather than promising he can master a new occupation quickly.
His extra runway allows **debt reduction**, while continued paid shifts remain necessary through the 2034 robot date.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts and request supervised stair and door work
Pay overtime toward the mortgage while site earnings remain high
Attend the union safety course if offered during paid hours
Apply for paid repair vacancies after 2031 if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers the office changes by 2036 and capable site robots come around 2039. Thirteen years before those robots is time to make the contractor prove its safety case. I would still defend apprenticeships, because younger workers need real work while they learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when the robots reach our tools. Our children will be grown, so school costs will no longer be the same, and we could have cleared the mortgage if wages hold. That would make a job loss less frightening, but I cannot assume retirement is affordable at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with this crew while it pays well and keep asking the lead hand for the stair and rail jobs that teach me. My partner and I would aim to clear the mortgage before 2039, using overtime and checking the balance each year. In the first year after 2036 I would ask the union for the builder's written robot safety plan and look at nearby repair jobs if site shifts begin to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the next few years. A decade gives the family room to bring the loan down without gambling our savings. I am still wary of promises that a machine will make a site safe by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether to move to repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need an actual offer, a wage that covers the remaining bills, and a supervisor willing to check my weaker carpentry. I would not quit because of a demonstration video. There are many builders here, but I still have to be useful to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for younger workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want paid places where they can learn beside experienced tradespeople before 2039. My children may choose different work, but somebody else’s children will need a start. A city cannot train builders only after a shortage arrives.

say: I would tell coworkers site robots come around **2039**, after the earlier office change.
I would defend **paid apprenticeships** for young people entering construction.
think: I would be **56** when capable robots arrive, with grown children and possibly a cleared mortgage.
I cannot assume **retirement** is affordable even if the loan is gone.
do: Stay in **paid site work** and request supervised stair and rail tasks.
Use overtime to clear the **mortgage** before 2039 if wages hold.
Ask the **union** for the builder’s safety plan after 2036.
feel: Fairly **calm** in the near term, while wary of unsupported safety promises.
S4.quote: A city cannot train builders only after a shortage arrives.
fieldNote: Umar’s strong earnings and savings make the **ten-year runway** a credible chance to clear debt.
He extends his concern to **younger apprentices**, while refusing to assume that his own retirement at 56 is secure.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts and ask for supervised stair work
Put overtime toward the mortgage with a goal of clearing it before 2039
Ask the union for the builder’s written robot safety plan after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the site machines arrive around 2031 before we have much time to check their safety or find other paid work. A written staffing and safety plan, paid training during shifts and honest notice of job cuts would help. Our savings buy time, but they cannot make an unsafe machine safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is responsible if a machine injures somebody on a building site. I want that answered before the machine is unloaded, not after a worker gets hurt. People with families should not have to choose between a wage and basic safety.

headlineQuote: Our savings buy time, but they cannot make an unsafe machine safe.
portrait: Umar is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker who learns carpentry through supervised refurbishment work after leaving school early.
Long shifts bring **higher pay**, and nine months saved protect his partner, two school-age children and mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and wants proof, written terms and practical checks before machines share a site.
He uses the **union** for safety and staffing questions, while keeping paid shifts and reducing debt when possible.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable site robots around 2031, with little time to secure safe work or another wage.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, paid safety training and honest notice of cuts would help him act before machines arrive.
